questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Sets That Are Not Vector Spaces
questions.problem:
Let $W$ be the set of all polynomials in the variable $x\in R$ with coefficients in $R$ of degree $5$ or greater. Complete the following sentence:

*$W$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to polynomials addition and multiplication of a polynomial by a real number) because $\text{_________}\,.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The correct answer is as follows:

*$W$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to polynomials addition and multiplication of a polynomial by a real number) because **$W$ does not contain the zero element.** *

Indeed, the zero polynomial has degree $0$, which is less than $5.$

On the other hand: 

- Addition of polynomials is associative. $\,✓$

- Addition of polynomials is commutative. $\,✓$

- Addition and scalar multiplication of polynomials satisfy the distributive laws. $\,✓$

- For any polynomial $p(x)$ of degree $5$ (or greater), the corresponding negative polynomial $-p(x)$ has the same degree. $\,✓$

$W$ does not contain the zero element

addition of polynomials is not associative

answer_fields.correct_value: $W$ does not contain the zero element

questions.problem:
Let $Y$ be the set of all polynomials in the variable $x\in R$ with coefficients in $R$ of degree exactly $2.$ Complete the following sentence:

*$Y$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to polynomials addition and multiplication of a polynomial by a real number) because $\text{_________}\,.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The correct answer is as follows:

*$Y$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to polynomials addition and multiplication of a polynomial by a real number) because **addition of polynomials in $Y$ is not closed.** *

Indeed, let's consider, for example, the polynomials $p(x)={x}^{2}+x$ and $q(x)=-{x}^{2}.$ Then $p,q\in Y,$ but 

$$
p(x)+q(x)={x}^{2}+x+(-{x}^{2})=x\notin Y
$$

 because $\operatorname{deg}⁡(p+q)=1\ne 2.$

On the other hand:

- $1\cdot p=p$ for all $p\in Y.$ $\,✓$

- Addition and scalar multiplication of polynomials satisfy the distributive laws. $\,✓$

- Addition of polynomials is commutative. $\,✓$

- Addition of polynomials is associative. $\,✓$

questions.problem:
Let $J$ be the set of purely imaginary complex numbers, that is, complex numbers of the form  $ai,$ where  $a$ is a nonzero real number. Complete the following sentence: 

*$J$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to addition of complex numbers and scalar multiplication of a complex number by a real number) because $\text{_________}\,.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The correct answer is as follows:

*$J$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to addition of complex numbers and scalar multiplication of a complex number by a real number) because **multiplication of $z\in J$ by real scalars is not closed.** *

For example, if $\alpha =0$ and $z=i,$ then $\alpha \cdot z=0\cdot i=0\notin J.$

On the other hand:

- Addition in $J$ is associative. $\,✓$

- Addition  in $J$ is commutative.  $\,✓$

- Addition and scalar multiplication in $J$ satisfy the distributive laws. $\,✓$

- If  $z\in J$ then $z=ai$ for some $a\in R.$ Hence, $-z=(-a)i\in J$   since $-a\in R.$ $\,✓$

questions.problem:
From top to bottom, fill in the blanks and hence complete the proof of the following statement using the axioms $[\text{A}1]-[\text{A}8]$ given below.

*Statement:*

*Given any $x\in V$, if $y$ is a vector such that $x+y=0$, then $y=-x.$* 

*Proof:*

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =0 &  & [\,\text{given}\,] \\ (x+y)+(-x) & =0+(-x) &  & [\,\text{add }-x\text{ to both sides}\,] \\ (y+x)+(-x) & =(-x)+0 &  & [\,\text{axiom A1}\,] \\ (y+x)+(-x) & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ y+(x+(-x)) & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ y+0 & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom A4}\,] \\ y & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom A3}\,]\end{aligned}
$$

The axioms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{[A1]}:x+y=y+x & \text{[A5]}:1\cdot x=x \\ \text{[A2]}:(x+y)+z=x+(y+z) & \text{[A6]}:\alpha (\beta x)=(\alpha \beta )x \\ \text{[A3]}:x+0=x & \text{[A7]}:(\alpha +\beta )x=\alpha x+\beta x \\ \text{[A4]}:x+(-x)=0 & \text{[A8]}:\alpha (x+y)=\alpha x+\alpha y\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the vector space axioms, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =0 &  & [\,\text{given}\,] \\ (x+y)+(-x) & =0+(-x) &  & [\,\text{add }-x\text{ to both sides}\,] \\ (y+x)+(-x) & =(-x)+0 &  & [\,\text{axiom A1}\,] \\ (y+x)+(-x) & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom }\text{A3}\,\,] \\ y+(x+(-x)) & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom }\text{A2}\,\,] \\ y+0 & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom A4}\,] \\ y & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom A3}\,]\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Sets That Are Not Vector Spaces
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $V$ be the set of all real polynomials of degree exactly $3$, equipped with the usual addition and scalar multiplication operations. Complete the following sentence:

*$V$ is **not** a vector space because $\textrm{_________}\,.$*

- the sum of two polynomials of degree $3$ may not be a polynomial of degree $3$

- $V$ does not contain the polynomial $-p(x)$ for every $p(x) \in V$

- addition of polynomials is not commutative
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The correct answer  is as follows:

*$V$ is **not** a vector space because **the sum of two polynomials of degree $3$ may not be a polynomial of degree $3$.** *

For instance, if $p(x) = 1 +x^3$ and $q(x) = 1-x^3$, then $p(x)$ and $q(x)$ are in $V.$ However  

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x)+q(x) & =(1+{x}^{3})+(1-{x}^{3}) \\  & =2\notin V.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand:

- Addition of polynomials is commutative.

- For any polynomial $p(x)$ of degree $3$, the corresponding negative polynomial $-p(x)$ also has degree $3.$
